all_of: user input is checked for forbidden characters and then passed through a normaliser before being used as a path
the normaliser can introduce a character the check rejected
any_of: a template include concatenates user input into a template name
a directory outside the upload root is writable by the worker
the filename is derived from a prefix of the content while the whole content is written

chain.action: read the sink first: find what turns stored data into a template or a path
chain.why: {% include "errors/" + error + ".html" %} with error from the query string is what makes a written file executable

chain.action: read the Dockerfile's permissions, not just the app
chain.why: chmod 1773 on templates/errors is the deliberate door; without it the traversal writes nowhere useful

chain.action: read the normaliser's source for rewrites that happen AFTER the application's own check
chain.why: werkzeug url_fix starts with s.replace(chr(92), '/'), so a backslash becomes a separator the filter already approved

chain.action: pad the prefix that forms the filename so the payload sits beyond it
chain.why: the name comes from content[:128] while the file receives the whole content; padding keeps the on-disk name clean and predictable

chain.action: write a template whose dangerous identifiers are supplied at render time from request parameters
chain.why: the payload itself is subject to the same character filter, so the dunders cannot be literal

first_confirming_probe.request: submit content that is only the traversal prefix built from backslashes, then read the redirect's Location header
first_confirming_probe.expected: the Location shows the path outside the upload directory, proving the normaliser produced separators the filter rejected
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: the Location still points inside the upload directory, so the normaliser leaves backslashes alone

blast_radius: this writes a file into the application's own template directory and the app offers no delete route. On a shared, always-on host the planted templates cannot be cleaned up, so name them uniquely and say so when reporting.

verification.evidence: the flag was rendered into the GET / response body by the include of the planted template

reuse_when: a filter runs before a normaliser, encoder or path builder that can reintroduce the blocked byte
a template name is concatenated from user input
a filename is derived from a prefix while the full input is stored
known_traps: the payload must satisfy the same character filter as the path, which rules out every literal __class__/__globals__ chain; pass the dunders in as request parameters and let jinja's getattr fall back to item lookup
cycler.__init__.__globals__ resolves to jinja2.utils and has no os; lipsum.__globals__ does
parameterise the module and every call so a wrong guess is a URL change, not another planted file
